query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A thermally induced oxide/spinel tribo-layer, facilitated by moderate-temperature annealing, is the primary mechanism governing wear resistance and local plastic flow in FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coatings during sliding at 600–800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate in the as-deposited condition.
generation.intervention: Introduce a short annealing step at 700 °C for 2 h in air after coating deposition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding tests from 600 to 800 °C at comparable load and speed in air.
generation.structural_mediator: A stable oxide/spinel tribo-layer formed upon moderate-temperature annealing.
generation.mechanism: Moderate-temperature annealing promotes incipient oxidation and microstructural refinement, facilitating the formation of a protective tribo-oxide or spinel film that reduces abrasive contact, improves wear resistance, and stabilizes dislocation structures under high-temperature sliding.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed coatings exhibit measurably lower wear rates and more uniform plastic deformation relative to unannealed references.
generation.boundary: Valid for 600–800 °C sliding contact under moderate loads and speeds in air.
generation.uncertainty: Exact oxide/spinel nature and its stability across different compositions and conditions remain partially unverified.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare an annealed coating group (700 °C, 2 h, in air) with an unannealed group under identical 600–800 °C sliding tests. Assess wear rate, friction coefficient, microstructural evolution, and tribo-layer formation.
measurements: Coefficient of friction over test duration
SEM/TEM cross-sectional images of worn surfaces
EDS or XPS characterization of oxide/spinel layers
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If annealed coatings fail to reduce wear or show similar/worse plastic deformation relative to unannealed coatings, then the hypothesized oxide/spinel film mechanism does not govern high-temperature wear and deformation.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract The microstructure, temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) were investigated. SLM-built HEA had a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase random solid solution. In addition, SLM-built HEA was composed of epitaxial growth grains, dislocation network and nano-sized oxides. Room- and high-temperature compression tests confirmed that SLM-built HEA has outstanding mechanical properties in all temperature ranges compared to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs reported up to the present. The excellent mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA were achieved with fine grains, high dislocation density and fine precipitates at low temperatures (25 °C to 600 °C), and by high dislocation density and fine precipitates at high temperatures (700 °C or higher). On the other hand, the deformation microstructure showed that slip and deformation twins are the main deformation mechanisms from 25 °C to 600 °C, and slip and partial recrystallization are the main deformation mechanisms above 700 °C. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), since their discovery by Yeh et al. in 2004, [1] have opened up researchers to a new alloy system that contains five or more equimolar principal elements. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, high entropy, and cocktail effects have been identified as the core effects contributing to the superior properties, hardness, strength, ductility, erosion, tribocorrosion, corrosion, and oxidation/wear resistance [5] − [7] of HEAs in a wide range of temperatures over conventional alloys. From the viewpoint of applications in extrusion dies and cutting inserts, the cost of metal powders used to develop bulk HEAs can hinder their commercialization as an alternative to the alloys in use. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . decision.trend: Recent tribological studies on high-entropy alloys (HEAs) such as AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 (PMC7515071) and CuMoTaWV coatings (PMC7304825) show that microstructure and thermally induced oxide or spinel tribofilms can strongly influence wear behavior at elevated temperatures. In AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5, wear was initially worse at moderate temperatures yet significantly improved above ~800 °C once protective tribo-oxides formed. Similarly, CuMoTaWV RHEA films exhibited better adhesion and wear performance after suitable thermal treatments. Meanwhile, high-temperature mechanical studies on CoCrFeMnNi (PMC7229066) demonstrated stable dislocation structures and strong mechanical performance up to ~700–800 °C, underscoring the potential of certain FCC-based HEAs to resist high-temperature deformation. Despite these findings, no single, unified mechanism has yet been established that definitively links the high-temperature formation of oxide layers, microstructural stability, and tribological performance in FeNiCrCoCu thin coatings during sliding.
decision.unsolved: Although evidence suggests that thermally activated processes—such as the formation of protective oxides or spinels and changes in microstructure—can reduce wear and alter the mode of plastic deformation in HEAs at high temperatures, it remains unclear which specific factor (grain-boundary sliding, interfacial tribo-layers, diffusion-controlled oxidation, or dislocation-mediated plasticity) governs both overall wear resistance and local deformation in FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
decision.lever: Introduce a short, moderate-temperature annealing step (e.g. 700 °C for 2 h in air) after coating deposition to promote incipient oxidation or microstructural ordering, then perform high-temperature (600–800 °C) sliding tests. Compare wear rates and in situ microscopic deformation signatures of the annealed vs. as-deposited baseline coatings under identical loads and speeds.
decision.why: If the friction-induced formation of a stable oxide or spinel tribo-layer, facilitated by microstructural refinement or partial surface oxidation during annealing, serves as the dominant mechanism controlling wear and deformation at 600–800 °C, then annealed coatings should exhibit lower wear rates and more uniform plastic flow. This aligns with prior findings (PMC7515071 and PMC7304825) that protective high-temperature films and microstructure adjustments enhance high-temperature tribological performance in HEAs and that plastic deformation in FCC-based alloys remains stable up to ~700–800 °C (PMC7229066). Should the annealed coating show no improvement—or show a worse response under these conditions—it would indicate that thermally induced oxide/spinel formation and grain-boundary control are not the primary governing mechanism, thereby falsifying the hypothesis.
